The synchrony of hatching events within a single clutch is often high, with multiple neonates emerging over a short window, likely an adaptation to reduce individual predation risk during the vulnerable transition to an aquatic existence.

Adult body sizes in Crocodylus palustris are strongly sexually dimorphic, a pattern common among crocodilians where larger males monopolize mating opportunities. This demographic structure makes the species particularly vulnerable to anthropogenic pressures such as habitat loss and poaching, as the removal of older, highly fecund adults can have a disproportionately large impact on population growth rates. Comparative analyses with other large crocodilians, such as the saltwater crocodile, indicate that the lifespan of the Mugger is broadly similar, reflecting a conserved pattern of slow senescence among apex predator reptiles in tropical and subtropical environments.
